title: "2.9.2 Modal Limits"

Van Hamme distinguishes three classes of necessity: logical-analytic (Class A), modal-structural (Class B), and existential (Class C), and argues that modal logic's jurisdiction stops at Class B. Arguments that ask modal apparatus to certify Class C necessity (that a particular being exists necessarily) cannot get that result without admitting Class B structure, which already does the work the proposed existent was supposed to do. Van Hamme reads the result as a limit on a family of necessary-being arguments; the present argument reads it as a relocation of modal force. What modal logic *can* deliver, Class B (modal-structural necessity, the necessity of frame-conditions any possible world satisfies), is the class T∧S∧Φ occupies. The identification is inclusive rather than exhaustive: Class B may include further frame-conditions the present argument does not develop, but T, S, and Φ are Class B necessities on the structural-minimum reading the present argument develops, since they are the frame-conditions any modally specifiable state of affairs satisfies. @fritzLoSchmid2026 run a structurally distinct reverse-direction modal ontological argument against a necessary-being conclusion, valid in S4 alone, without reliance on the Euclidean Axiom. The relevant comparison is with the fixed-domain modal-stability argument and its Bottleneck defense at §§2.1.4–2.1.5, not with §2.1.3's non-vacuity lemma. Any claim that an S4-only reverse argument transfers to the present framework must be assessed against those premises rather than attributed to Modal Constitution. Three independent lines converge on the negative result: modal logic does not by itself deliver a particular necessary being. The present argument adds the positive complement: what modal logic does deliver is Nature.
